title: The Ancient Machine That Predicted the Sky — and Jammed in Months
parts: In nineteen hundred, sponge divers near a Greek island found a shipwreck, forty-five meters down.
Inside it: a corroded lump of bronze.
Nobody noticed the gears for almost a year.
It turned out to be the most precise calculating machine of the ancient world.
We will mark every claim: documented, disputed, or myth.
By the end, you will hear what this machine actually calculated.
You will also find out why the most famous claim about who built it probably is not true — and why a two thousand twenty-five study says it may have jammed within months.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
The wreck lies off the Greek island of Antikythera, near Point Glyphadia, forty-five meters down.
Sponge divers from the island of Simi, led by captain Dimitrios Kontos, found it in nineteen hundred. The mechanism itself was recovered around nineteen oh one.
Nobody realized it held gears until May seventeenth, nineteen oh two, when the archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed them.
Nobody agrees on exactly when or where it was built. Candidates run from the late second century B.C. into the following century; the workshop's location is still debated too.
Documented — except the exact date and place, which stay unverified.
One Roman writer may be to blame for the most repeated claim about this machine.
Cicero, writing in the first century B.C., described two machines built by Archimedes, and a third built "recently" by Posidonius — all showing the sun, the moon, and five planets.
Documented. That is what Cicero wrote.
So, was this the Archimedes machine?
Probably not.
Archimedes' own machines were still in Rome at least thirty years after this ship likely sank.
The Archimedes story is a popular reading of Cicero's words — not proof that this is the object he was writing about.
Our reading: a famous name probably got attached to a mysterious object by association, not by evidence.
Myth.
In twenty twenty-one, engineers at University College London built a digital model of the front gearing.
Their model lines up Venus's four hundred sixty-two year cycle with a sixty-three-tooth gear. They say it is the first model that fits all the surviving evidence and the inscriptions.
As of that paper, the model existed only on a computer. It is still unverified whether anyone has physically built and tested it since.
Documented, with that limit noted.
This was not the first attempt to rebuild it, either.

A simple model in the nineteen seventies. The first working model, built in two thousand two. Mechanical pieces machined from C.T. scans in twenty eighteen. And one digital-only design from twenty twelve, never built physically.
Four separate attempts, four different designs — not one machine steadily improving.
Documented.
In twenty twenty-four, a team at the University of Glasgow ran statistical models on the spacing of holes in the calendar ring.
Their best estimate: three hundred fifty-four or three hundred fifty-five holes — a lunar calendar, not a three-hundred-sixty-five-day solar one.
Documented.
Then, in twenty twenty-five, a different team simulated the gears themselves.

Their finding: the triangular tooth shape, combined with manufacturing errors beyond what the design could tolerate, meant the mechanism could only be wound forward for about four months before the teeth jammed.
Disputed. The full technical paper was not read in full for this video — only its summary and two independent press reports.
One more caution, from the people who covered that study.
Two thousand years of corrosion may have warped the parts well beyond their original shape, so today's measurements might not match the machine when it was new.

Our reading: put the twenty twenty-four calendar study next to the twenty twenty-five jamming study, and you get neither a perfect machine nor a useless one — a finely designed calendar that its own manufacturing may not have been able to sustain.
Headlines calling it "a machine that never worked" go too far. The real finding is about jamming and needing a reset, not total failure. Myth, stated that bluntly.
Let's count what we actually know.
A precision astronomical calculator, built by someone, somewhere, in the ancient Mediterranean: documented.
Whether it ran reliably for years without jamming: disputed.
That it was built by Archimedes himself: myth.
So, more than two thousand years later, who actually built this machine?
Nobody knows, exactly. We know what it could calculate — not who designed it, or whether it ever ran smoothly for more than a few months at a time.
